clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant disorder combining cerebellar ataxia with an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, reflected in its descriptive name sensorimotor neuropathy with ataxia (SMNA).
Distinguished from the purely sensory dominant ataxias by prominent motor involvement — distal muscle weakness and atrophy accompany the sensory loss.
Linked to a locus on the long arm of chromosome 7 (7q22-q32); a missense variant in IFRD1 has been proposed as the candidate gene in the index family.
Onset is often in adolescence or early adulthood, with gait ataxia, dysarthria and nystagmus.
Reflexes are typically reduced or absent, while extensor plantar responses may appear, indicating mixed peripheral and central involvement.
MRI shows cerebellar atrophy and nerve conduction studies confirm an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy with neurogenic features.
The phenotype was originally characterised in an African-American kindred.
reference.pathophysiology: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 18, also termed sensorimotor neuropathy with ataxia, is an autosomal dominant condition mapped to chromosome 7q22-q32, with a missense change in IFRD1 (interferon-related developmental regulator 1) implicated as the underlying defect in the family in which it was defined, although the gene has not been robustly confirmed across independent cohorts. IFRD1 helps regulate transcriptional programmes in neuronal and muscle tissue, and its dysfunction is thought to produce degeneration of cerebellar pathways alongside sensory and motor peripheral nerves, yielding the characteristic combination of cerebellar atrophy, an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy and neurogenic muscle wasting. This dual central and peripheral, motor-involving pathology sets SCA18 apart from subtypes with a predominantly sensory neuronopathy such as SCA4 and SCA25.
additionalDifferentials: SCA4 (ZFHX3, 16q22) — dominant ataxia with a predominantly sensory neuropathy
SCA25 (PNPT1, 2p) — dominant ataxia with sensory neuronopathy, sometimes with gastrointestinal symptoms
Common repeat-expansion ataxias SCA1, SCA2 and SCA3, which may include peripheral neuropathy
Friedreich ataxia (recessive sensorimotor involvement with areflexia)
Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathies with ataxic features
Acquired chronic sensorimotor axonal neuropathies with coincidental cerebellar signs
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing or linkage to the 7q locus and IFRD1 where available
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography showing an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy with neurogenic changes
Hereditary ataxia and inherited-neuropathy gene panels
Bloods to exclude acquired causes of sensorimotor neuropathy (glucose and glycated haemoglobin, vitamin B12, paraprotein screen)
Family pedigree analysis with genetic counselling
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting motor neuron disease or an inflammatory neuropathy rather than SCA18.
Frequent falls arising from the combination of ataxia and limb weakness.
Subacute onset that should prompt a search for an acquired neuropathy.
reference.prognosis: Slowly progressive over years, with disability resulting from the combination of ataxia, distal weakness and sensory loss; lifespan is generally preserved.
pitfalls: Mistaking the condition for an isolated Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy or a pure cerebellar ataxia when both components are present.
Assuming the IFRD1 variant is confirmed in every family, when the causative gene remains provisional.
Overlooking the motor component, which is the key distinguishing feature from sensory-predominant dominant ataxias.
Failing to exclude common acquired sensorimotor neuropathies before invoking a rare hereditary diagnosis.
